written.myAnswer: Down the group, alkali-metal atoms become larger, so their outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and the metallic bonding becomes weaker. The metals are therefore softer and easier to cut.
Potassium reacts vigorously with halogens, forming ionic potassium halides.
Bromide ions, Br⁻, in sodium bromide are the reducing agent. They are oxidised to Br₂.
Iodine molecules are relatively large and have stronger intermolecular attractions than those of the lighter halogens, so iodine is solid at room temperature.
Nickel provides a surface on which hydrogen and oil are adsorbed. This brings them into contact and helps hydrogen add to the oil’s unsaturated bonds.
Helium has the lowest boiling point because its atoms are very small and the intermolecular attractions between them are weakest.
Alkali metals react with chlorine to form metal chlorides. The reactions become more vigorous down the group.
Strong metallic bonding holds metal atoms together, so metals are generally solids. Non-metals usually have weaker attractions between their particles and can exist as gases or solids.
Bromine, mercury and gallium are examples; gallium melts just above ordinary room temperature.
Transition elements commonly show variable oxidation states, form coloured compounds and act as catalysts, among other characteristic properties.
Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine and can oxidise bromide ions to bromine.

Fluorine is the most reactive halogen and iodine the least reactive. Fluorine atoms are smallest and have the greatest tendency to gain an electron; iodine atoms are largest and have the least tendency to gain one.

A catalytic converter uses catalysts such as platinum, palladium and rhodium to convert harmful exhaust gases—carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons—into less harmful products such as carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water.

Down Group 1, the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and is lost more easily, so reactivity increases. Down the halogen group, atoms become larger and have a weaker tendency to gain an electron, so reactivity decreases.

Metals have strong metallic bonding between positive ions and delocalised electrons, which makes them generally strong and tough. Non-metals lack this metallic bonding and are generally brittle or weak.
Alkali metals lose one electron to form positive ions, whereas halogens gain one electron to form negative ions. The oppositely charged ions can combine to form ionic compounds.
The H–Br bond is longer and weaker than the H–Cl bond because bromine atoms are larger than chlorine atoms. Hydrogen bromide therefore decomposes more readily on heating.

Metals are generally lustrous, malleable and ductile, conduct heat and electricity well, and are mostly solids with relatively high melting points. Non-metals are generally dull, brittle when solid, poor conductors, and may be gases or solids with relatively lower melting points.
Vanadium(V) oxide is less expensive than platinum and is less easily poisoned by impurities, while still catalysing the oxidation of sulphur dioxide.
Liquid sodium carries heat from the reactor core to the steam-generating system. Its good heat-conducting ability is used for this purpose.

Lithium behaves differently because its atoms and Li⁺ ions are very small and have high charge density. It forms some compounds with greater covalent character, reacts with nitrogen to form lithium nitride, and shows a diagonal relationship with magnesium.
Aluminium conducts heat well and forms a protective oxide layer, making it suitable for cooking utensils. Magnesium is more reactive and can burn readily, so it is less suitable.
